title: Pointers & References
unlocks: Understanding the code you already wrote.
objective: Go back and understand the pointer and the reference you used at Stage 5 without explanation. Then rewrite your CLI to drive the game through ttt::Game, so your terminal game and your web game run the exact same code path.
creates: a const& pass on everything from Stage 2 onwards

cpp: references cannot be null or rebound
why returning a reference to a local is a bug

notYet: how virtual dispatch works under the hood
checks: All the Stage 5 contract tests still pass.
All the Stage 2 and Stage 4 behaviour checks still pass.
Your CLI, rebuilt with AddressSanitizer, plays a full scripted game and exits clean.
Two games created at once stay independent (no globals).
hints: At Stage 5 you wrote `std::unique_ptr<ttt::Game>` and returned one from createGame(). Why a pointer at all? What would go wrong if createGame() returned a ttt::Game by value?
When you pass a std::array<char, 9> to a function by value, the whole array is copied. Print the address of the array inside and outside the function (`&arr`) and you can watch it happen.

void show(const Board& b)   // no copy, and show() cannot modify b
void apply(Board& b, int cell) // no copy, and apply() CAN modify b
Board  copyOf(Board b)         // a copy, usually not what you want

A reference is another name for an existing object: it must be bound when created and can never be re-bound. A pointer is a variable holding an address: it can be null and can be re-pointed. Use a reference when the thing definitely exists; use a pointer when 'nothing' is a legal answer, or when you are handing over ownership.

`ttt::Game& g = *game;` takes the unique_ptr's object and gives you a plain reference to it, which is why the rest of your CLI can use `g.play(...)` with a dot.

prompts.title: Explain this AddressSanitizer report
prompts.body:
I built my program with -fsanitize=address,undefined and got this:

<PASTE THE FULL REPORT>

Read it back to me from the top: what kind of error, what operation went wrong, and which frame in the stack is MY code rather than the standard library. Then ask me what I think the lifetime of that object was. Do not tell me the fix yet.

prompts.title: Review my use of references
prompts.body:
I have just gone through my tic-tac-toe code changing pass-by-value to pass-by-const-reference.

Here are my files:
<PASTE THEM>

Ask me questions. Specifically: for each parameter I changed, does the function need to modify it (& ) or only read it (const&) or actually want its own copy; and is there anywhere I now hold a reference to something that might not outlive it? Do not rewrite my code.

prompts.title: Quiz me on pointers and lifetime
prompts.body:
Quiz me on pointers, references, and object lifetime in C++ -- the things interviewers actually ask.

One question at a time, wait for my answer. Cover: the difference between a reference and a pointer, when a reference can be null (trick question), what std::unique_ptr guarantees, what a dangling reference is, and stack versus heap lifetime. If I answer vaguely, ask me to be precise about WHAT object exists and for HOW LONG.
